title: Pip and the Prize Pumpkin
markdown:
It’s a humdinger, a real knee-slapper with a bit of oomph, and it belongs to Pip, a champion worrier. Pip worried about everything. Did the sun know it was supposed to rise? It did. Were there enough clouds for shapes? There usually were. Would his toast land butter-side down? It often did, but it was never the end of the world. Pip’s biggest worry, though, was about his grandpa’s prize-winning pumpkin.

Grandpa Bert was famous, not movie-star famous, but small-town-famous for winning the Harvest Festival ribbon every single year. And this year’s pumpkin? It was the biggest, roundest, most glorious pumpkin ever. It sat on a velvet cushion, practically glowing. Pip, though, saw only a giant vulnerable target for everything. He imagined squirrels with tiny wrecking balls, or a sneaky tornado, or a grumpy badger thinking it was a comfy chair. You know, normal Pip thoughts.

One blustery Tuesday, just days before the festival, Grandpa Bert called Pip over. “Pip, my boy,” he boomed, “I need you to take Pumpkin Pete — yes, that’s his name — to the Whispering Woods. A special dewdrop falls on the Whispering Willow before the festival. They say it makes pumpkins extra prize-winningly spectacular.” He winked. Pip’s stomach did a triple somersault. The Whispering Woods? With a giant pumpkin? His pumpkin? This was worse than the butter-side-down toast incident of ’22.

“But… Grandpa,” Pip stammered, his voice a tiny squeak. “What if Pete gets boo-booed?”

Grandpa Bert chuckled. “Nonsense, Pip. You’ll be fine. Just remember: a brave heart can handle anything. And take Hywel.” He whistled, and a small fluffy creature with enormous surprised eyes hopped out. This was Hywel, Grandpa Bert’s garden gnome. Hywel didn’t talk, but he was good at carrying things and looking worried. Pip’s constant worrying was about to get a serious workout.

With Pumpkin Pete balanced on a cart, and Hywel wobbling beside him, Pip set off. The path to the Whispering Woods was a muddly-suggestion-of-a-path, and the trees seemed to whisper secrets. The wind went whoosh, making Pip jump. The leaves went rustle, rustle, and Pip imagined them as tiny sneaky hands. He clutched the cart handle so tightly his knuckles turned white. Hywel just looked more surprised than usual.

Suddenly they heard it. A low rumbling growl. Pip froze, his eyes wide. This was it. He squeezed his eyes shut, bracing for impact. Hywel let out a little eep.

But the growl wasn’t angry. It was hungry. And it was coming from behind a very large rock. Cautiously, Pip peeked. There, looking forlorn, was a furry creature with long drooping ears, gnawing on a dry twig. It looked like Hywel’s long-lost cousin, if that cousin had lost his spark. This was Grumbles, a Grizelda known for its perpetual bad mood.

“Are you going to eat Pete?” Pip whispered, trembling.

Grumbles sighed, a sound like a deflating balloon. “Eat a pumpkin? Why would I eat a pumpkin? It’s far too round. No, I’m hungry for happiness. For a smile. I haven’t seen one of those in ages.” Grumbles’s ears drooped even further. Pip, for the first time, forgot to worry about Pete. He just saw a sad creature.

Worrying about what might happen was keeping him from seeing what was happening. He looked at Grumbles, then at Pete, then at Hywel. “Well,” Pip said, a tiny bit of bravery bubbling up. “We can’t have that. Can we, Hywel?” Hywel nodded hopefully.

“Tell you what, Grumbles,” Pip said, his voice gaining confidence. “You help us get Pete to the Whispering Willow, and I’ll bring you back a slice of Grandpa Bert’s famous apple pie. It’s supposed to make even the grumpiest grin.”

Grumbles blinked its sad big eyes. “Apple pie?” it rumbled. “And you promise to bring it? You won’t forget?”

“Cross my heart and hope to not worry too much,” Pip declared. Hywel gave a happy wiggle.

This is where it got really interesting. Grumbles nudged the cart with its nose. Thump. It was a gentle nudge, but it sent Pete rolling downhill. Pip yelled and chased after it, Hywel scrambling behind. Grumbles, surprisingly agile, bounded ahead, expertly guiding Pete away from a giant spiky bush and towards the shimmering Whispering Willow. If Pete got scratched, no blue ribbon. Pip was no longer just the worrier, but the problem-solver, even when things went haywire.

They reached the Whispering Willow, its long branches dripping with sparkly tears. Just as the sun hit Pete, a single perfect dewdrop landed squarely on its stem. It shimmered, then sank into the pumpkin, making it gleam with an inner light.

“Hooray,” Pip cheered, a huge grin spreading across his face. Hywel did a little jig. Even Grumbles managed a faint lopsided smile.

Back home, Pete sat proudly on the velvet cushion, glowing brighter than ever. Grandpa Bert beamed. “You did it, Pip,” he boomed. Pip, holding a steaming slice of apple pie, watched Grumbles gobble it down, a genuine wide smile on its face.

At the Harvest Festival, Pumpkin Pete was a sensation. He took home the grand prize, of course, but Pip didn’t even notice the ribbon that much. He was too busy watching Grumbles, who was happily sharing pie with Hywel. Pip realized something important that day. Worrying was like a tangled ball of yarn; it just got more knotted. But facing things, and helping others? That felt like untangling the yarn, one stitch at a time. And sometimes you even ended up with a delicious slice of pie and a new, slightly less grumpy friend. That, Pip decided, was worth more than any prize. He still worried sometimes, of course. But now Pip knew that a brave heart, and a good slice of pie, could handle almost anything. And if his toast landed butter-side down? Well, that was just an invitation to a quick crumb-snatching race with Hywel.
